Two kinds of loop An algorithm can go round a loop. A repeat loop goes round a counted number of times. A forever loop never stops on its own. Press Next . An algorithm can go round a loop. A repeat loop goes round a counted number of times. A forever loop never stops on its own. Press Next . A loop is a part of an algorithm that happens again and again. Repeat 4 times is count-controlled: it counts to 4 and stops. Forever is indefinite: it has no count, so it goes round until something outside stops it. Brushing teeth: repeat 4 times, brush the top, brush the bottom. Four turns, then it stops. Traffic lights: forever, red, red and amber, green, amber. They never finish on their own. Children think forever means broken. It means the algorithm is meant to keep going: lights, a clock, a game loop. Press Next.

Follow the loops Follow each algorithm, tapping the step that comes next. Watch the counter go round the repeat loop; press Stop when the forever loop has gone round twice. Follow each algorithm, tapping the step that comes next. Watch the counter go round the repeat loop; press Stop when the forever loop has gone round twice. Following a loop means going back to its first step when you reach its last, and counting the turns. Repeat 4 times, brush top, brush bottom: top, bottom, top, bottom, top, bottom, top, bottom. Then rinse. Forever, red, red and amber, green, amber: round and round. Nothing in the loop stops it, so you press Stop. Children leave the loop after one turn. Read the count. Four times means four turns. Tap the next step, round and round.

Correct the loop One step INSIDE each loop is wrong, so it goes wrong every time round. Find it, fix it, and watch the corrected algorithm run. One step INSIDE each loop is wrong, so it goes wrong every time round. Find it, fix it, and watch the corrected algorithm run. A wrong step inside a loop is worse than one outside: it happens on every turn. Repeat 3 times: fill the can, pour on a plant, tip the can upside down. Every plant gets watered and then the water goes on the floor. Fix the one step and all three turns are fixed. Children fix the step outside the loop because it is easier to see. Look at what happens every turn. Tap the wrong step, choose the fix, watch.

Repetition makes it concise Written out long, the plant algorithm is 11 steps. With a repeat loop it is 5. Tap each reason a loop is better. Written out long, the plant algorithm is 11 steps. With a repeat loop it is 5. Tap each reason a loop is better. Repetition - a loop - makes an algorithm more concise: the same job in fewer steps. Fill, pour, walk, three times over, is nine steps written out. Repeat 3 times, fill, pour, walk, is three steps and a count. Shorter to read, shorter to write, and one change inside the loop changes every turn. Tap all four.

Repeat, or forever? Is this loop count-controlled (repeat, then stop) or indefinite (forever, until stopped)? Is this loop count-controlled (repeat, then stop) or indefinite (forever, until stopped)? Count-controlled: it knows how many times. Indefinite: it goes on until something outside stops it. Read, decide, tap.

steps.t: Where does the loop leave Robo? Robo's program has a repeat loop in it. Unroll it in your head, tap the square where Robo will stop, then press Go . Robo's program has a repeat loop in it. Unroll it in your head, tap the square where Robo will stop, then press Go . To predict a looped program, unroll the loop: do the body that many times in your head, following Robo's facing as you go. Repeat 2 times: forward, forward. That is forward four times. Repeat 3 times: forward, turn right, forward, turn left. Each turn moves Robo one up and one along, like stairs. Children do the loop body once. Count the turns on your fingers, and watch the arrow. Unroll it, tap the square, press Go.

Find the repeat Making four pancakes, written out long. Tap the steps of the FIRST pancake; the page folds the rest into one repeat. Making four pancakes, written out long. Pour, cook, flip, cook, plate. Four times. Written once with repeat 4 times: five steps instead of twenty. Tap the five steps of the first pancake.

Which algorithm is best? Three algorithms get you from home to school. Each round names a purpose . Tap the algorithm that suits it best. Three algorithms get you from home to school. The main road is free and dry but has the most steps. Children pick one favourite for every purpose. The purpose changes the answer. Read it every time. Read the purpose, compare the facts, tap.

Outcome: does it really do the whole job, and how well? Tap all four.

What decomposition is Decomposition means breaking a big task into parts. In an algorithm each part is a sub-routine : a small algorithm with a name. Tap each idea. Decomposition means breaking a big task into parts. In an algorithm each part is a sub-routine : a small algorithm with a name. Tap each idea. A sub-routine is a named part of an algorithm. The main algorithm says do WASH, and WASH is its own list of steps somewhere else. Getting ready for school: main algorithm - do WASH, do DRESS, do BREAKFAST, do BAG, leave. WASH: face, teeth, hair. DRESS: shirt, trousers, socks, shoes. Each is short, named, and can be reused. Children think a sub-routine is a shortcut that skips steps. It skips nothing. All the steps are still there, in the sub-routine. Tap all four.

steps.h: Which sub-routine does it belong to?
steps.t: Which sub-routine does it belong to? Decompose 'a school morning' into four sub-routines. Put each step into the sub-routine it belongs to. Decompose 'a school morning' into four sub-routines. Put each step into the sub-routine it belongs to. Decomposing is deciding which steps belong together, and giving each group a name. Teeth, face, hair: WASH. Shirt, socks, shoes: DRESS. Bowl, cereal, milk: BREAKFAST. Books, lunch, coat: BAG. Read the step, tap its sub-routine.

Write the main algorithm Now the main algorithm: it calls the sub-routines in order. Tap the calls in the order a school morning happens. Now the main algorithm: it calls the sub-routines in order. Tap the calls in the order a school morning happens. The main algorithm is short: one call per sub-routine, in the right order, and the odd step of its own. Do WASH, do DRESS, do BREAKFAST, do BAG, leave the house. Five lines, and behind them twenty steps. Children put BAG before BREAKFAST. BAG ends with your coat on and your bag in your hand: it is the last thing before the door. Tap what comes first.

Follow the calls Follow the main algorithm. When it says do a sub-routine, tap the call, then that sub-routine's steps, then carry on where you left off. Follow the main algorithm. When it says do a sub-routine, tap the call, then that sub-routine's steps, then carry on where you left off. Following an algorithm with a sub-routine means jumping into the sub-routine, doing all its steps, and jumping back to the line after the call. Main: do WASH. Jump in: face, teeth, hair. Jump back: do DRESS. Jump in: shirt, trousers, socks, shoes. Back again. Children forget to come back and carry on. After the last step of a sub-routine, the next step is the line after its call. Tap the call, the steps, then carry on.

Why sub-routines help The same WASH sub-routine appeared in the morning AND at bedtime. Tap each reason sub-routines help. The same WASH sub-routine appeared in the morning AND at bedtime. Tap each reason sub-routines help. A sub-routine is written once and used in many places, so a change to it changes every place at once. Add 'floss' to WASH and both the morning and bedtime algorithms get it, without editing either. The main algorithm stays short enough to read in one look. Someone else can write DRESS while you write WASH. Tap all four.

If this, then that An algorithm can have a fork in it: IF something is true, do these steps; otherwise do those. The input decides. Tap each one. An algorithm can have a fork in it: IF something is true, do these steps; otherwise do those. The input decides. Tap each one. A branch is a choice inside an algorithm. The same algorithm gives a different output for a different input. IF it is raining, take an umbrella; otherwise take sunglasses. The weather is the input; what you carry is the output. IF the kettle has boiled, pour; otherwise wait. IF the answer is right, say well done; otherwise say try again. Children think the algorithm changed. The algorithm is the same. The input changed, so it took the other branch. Tap all five.

Take the branch Choose an input, then follow the algorithm through the branch that input takes. Then try the other input. Choose an input, then follow the algorithm through the branch that input takes. Then try the other input. Following a branch: do the steps before the IF, then ONLY the branch that matches the input, then the steps after. Raining: get dressed, take the umbrella, walk to school. Dry: get dressed, take sunglasses, walk to school. Same start, same end, different middle. Children do both branches. Only one branch runs. The other is skipped completely. Pick an input, follow the branch, then pick the other.

Write the branch Now you write one. Choose the question the algorithm must ask, put every step where it belongs, then test it with both inputs. Now you write one. Choose the question the algorithm must ask, put every step where it belongs, then test it with both inputs. Writing an algorithm with a branch: decide what happens every time, and what happens only for one answer to the question. Borrowing a book: look on the shelf first, every time. On the shelf: take it to the desk and scan your card. Not there: ask for it to be saved. Then say thank you, every time. Test it with both answers. One algorithm, two inputs, two different outputs. Children put a step that happens for both answers inside one branch. If it happens whatever the answer, it goes outside the branches: first, or after. Choose the question, then tap a step and tap Put it here. Then Test it.

steps.h: Build an algorithm with a repeat
steps.t: Build an algorithm with a repeat The task needs the same steps done several times. Put those steps in the repeat box, set how many times, and run it. The task needs the same steps done several times. Put those steps in the repeat box, set how many times, and run it. Developing an algorithm with repetition means spotting what repeats, putting it in a loop, and setting the count. Water 3 plants: repeat 3 times, fill the can, pour on a plant, walk to the next. Then put the can away. The page unrolls your loop and checks it does the whole task, not more and not less. Children put 'get the can' inside the loop. You get the can once. Only what happens for every plant goes in the loop. Tap steps into the box, set the count, run.

steps.h: In the loop, or outside it?
steps.t: In the loop, or outside it? For 'water all the plants in the garden', does this step go INSIDE the repeat loop or OUTSIDE it? For 'water all the plants in the garden', does this step go INSIDE the repeat loop or OUTSIDE it? Inside the loop: anything that happens for every plant. Outside: anything that happens once, before or after. Read, decide, tap.

The repeat block A program can repeat too. The repeat block runs the block after it that many times. Press Next . A program can repeat too. The repeat block runs the block after it that many times. Press Next . Repetition in a program is a repeat block: repeat 3 times, jump, makes the cat jump three times. Each time round is one iteration. Repeat 3 times, jump: jump, jump, jump. Repeat 4 times, move right: four squares to the right, one per iteration. Children think the repeat block repeats the whole program. It repeats the ONE block after it. The loops in lessons 1 and 4 held several steps, and in many apps a repeat can hold several blocks; this one holds one. Press Next.

Build it with a repeat Read the algorithm and build the program. When it says a number of times, use a repeat block, then Run it. Read the algorithm and build the program. When it says a number of times, use a repeat block, then Run it. When the algorithm says 'jump 4 times', that is a repeat block and one jump, not four jumps. Jump 4 times, say hello: repeat 4 times, jump, say hello. Three blocks. Go home, move right 3 times, grow: go home, repeat 3 times, move right, grow. Children drag four jump blocks. It works, but it is not the program the algorithm asked for. Use the repeat. Read, build with a repeat, run.

Fold it into a loop Each program works but repeats itself block by block. Fold the repeats into repeat blocks and take out the waits, then Run it to check it still does the same. Each program works but repeats itself block by block. Fold the repeats into repeat blocks and take out the waits, then Run it to check it still does the same. A program that writes grow, grow, grow can write repeat 3 times, grow instead. Same output, fewer blocks. Grow, grow, grow, wait, say hello: repeat 3 times grow, say hello. Run it. The cat grows three times and says hello, exactly as before. Children fold two different blocks into one repeat. Only the SAME block, back to back, can be folded. Tap a block, choose, run, check.

Why comment your code? A comment is a note beside a block that says what it is for. The computer ignores it; people read it. Tap each benefit. A comment is a note beside a block that says what it is for. The computer ignores it; people read it. Tap each benefit. A comment is written for a person, not the computer. It says what a block is for, or why it is there. 'Reset the cat' beside go home. 'Do the jump three times' beside the repeat. Next week you will have forgotten why the wait is there. The comment remembers. A partner reading your program understands it faster. Children write a comment that repeats the block: 'jump' beside jump. Say WHY: 'jump over the wall'. Tap all four.

A comment sits beside the block it explains. Match each note to its block. 'Put the cat back at the start' explains go home. 'Do the next block three times' explains the repeat. 'Greet the player when the jumps are done' explains say hello. Tap a comment, tap its block.

Good comment, or not? A good comment says WHY a block is there, or what it is for. Is this a good comment? A good comment says WHY a block is there, or what it is for. Is this a good comment? Good: it says why, or what for. Not good: it repeats the block's own words, or it is wrong. Read, decide, tap.
